title: Toward less
hookLine: to Mahapajapati: what leads to less, not more, is the teaching

lines: A NUN, ABOUT TO GO ALONE.
cards: Mahapajapati Gotami was the Buddha's aunt. Tradition says that after his mother died she raised him as her own son, and that years later she was the first woman ordained as a nun, leading the women who followed her.
In this sutta she comes with a short request: teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard it, I can go and live alone, diligent and resolute. Not a long discourse.
A rule of thumb she can carry into solitude, and what she gets is a test she can apply to anything.

teach.b: Gotami, the Buddha says, whatever things you know lead to passion, not to dispassion; to bondage, not to release; to piling up, not to letting go; to wanting much, not wanting little; to discontent, not contentment; to crowding together, not solitude; to laziness, not energy; to being a burden, not being easy to support: of those you can be sure, this is not the Dhamma, not the discipline, not the teacher's instruction.
And whatever leads the other way, to dispassion, release, letting go, wanting little, contentment, solitude, energy and being easy to support: of that you can be sure, this is the Dhamma.
Eight pairs, all pointing the same direction. Notice what he didn't give her: not a list of doctrines to check, not an authority to obey. A test by results.
Look at where a thing leads.
Toward more grasping, more crowding, more needing? Be careful.
Toward less? That's the way. It's portable, too.

Gotami can take it into the forest and use it on anything: a habit, a friendship, a teacher's advice, even a meditation practice. And it's gentle. Toward less doesn't mean nothing; it means the direction of travel.
A little less wanting than yesterday is already the path. Put it next to yesterday's goldsmith: balance for the household, and for a nun heading into solitude, the needle tilting toward less.

how: Buddhist teachers often quote the brief teaching to Mahapajapati as a test for any practice or idea, and in the Theravada forest tradition 'wanting little' and contentment are held up as everyday monastic virtues.

o: eating only one small meal each day
heading toward fewer wants, not more
giving away everything you own at once

p: the Buddha's aunt, who asked in brief

s: Mahapajapati raised the Buddha after his mother died
tradition says so: she was his aunt and became his foster mother.
the Buddha gave her a long list of doctrines to memorize
he gave her a test by results: see where a thing leads.
the test says solitude and energy are signs of the Dhamma
they're among the eight things the teaching leads toward.

games.q: you're Mahapajapati, about to live alone. you ask for a teaching in brief. what do you get?
o: a test: what leads toward less is the Dhamma.
a rule to stay near the community.
games.why: a test you can carry anywhere: look at where a thing leads. toward letting go and wanting little, it's the teaching; toward more, it isn't.

practice: Let one urge come to mind, from today or one that comes back often: another scroll, another snack, another purchase, another opinion.

Without pushing it away, ask the Buddha's question, where does this lead, toward more wanting or less, and feel the answer in the body. Then breathe out slowly, and imagine one small step toward less.

wordCard.voice: Toward less. The Buddha's brief teaching to Mahapajapati Gotami: whatever leads to letting go, wanting little and contentment, that is the Dhamma. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali appicchata: 'fewness of wishes,' wanting little, one of the marks of the Dhamma in AN 8.53.

carryVoice: Your line: where does this lead? It's a question that fits in a pocket and goes anywhere. See you tomorrow.
